name: Vera Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Vera. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and also what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior buyer at Cresta Packaging, a distributor that supplies takeaway boxes, coffee cups, napkins and cling film to cafés, caterers and market traders. I buy the paper and card lines, mostly from two big mills and a few importers. I use an AI assistant all day: it reads the supplier price sheets, drafts my emails and flags when a container from overseas is running late. I love the deal-making, and I don't love how slow head office is to let juniors make decisions.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a slow decision look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Last month I found a cheaper supplier for kraft paper bags, about eight percent less, and it took three weeks for my manager, Philip, to sign it off. By then the price had gone up. I'm still learning, so I understand why they check, but it drives me mad. My husband Daniel drives a delivery lorry, and between us we've got under a month of savings, because we just paid for our wedding and a deposit on our flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five short pictures of the future. The first is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, the tools are good helpers but they don't replace good judgement. I'd post something about how hard work and a bit of hustle still matter. At church I'd say the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a little disappointed, because I was hoping AI would let someone like me move faster than the people with degrees. My job's safe, but the pay is still low and we've got nothing saved after the wedding. Daniel's overtime is what keeps us afloat some months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI every day and push to get my own sign-off limit, so I can close deals myself. I'd start a small side business on weekends, selling eco packaging to market traders I already know. And we'd rebuild the savings, a little every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. Restless, and a bit tight on money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the side business look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buying compostable boxes in bulk and selling smaller packs to food stalls. The big distributors won't sell compostable boxes under a thousand units. I already know half the stallholders at the Saturday market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't Cresta mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Philip first, and I'd only sell to stalls too small for Cresta to bother with. If he said no, I wouldn't do it. I don't go behind people's backs.

I'd post that **hard work** and a bit of hustle still matter.
think: I hoped AI would help me **move faster** than people with degrees.
Pay is low and we have **nothing saved** after the wedding.
do: Push for my own **sign-off limit** to close deals myself.
Start a weekend business selling **eco packaging** to market traders.
feel: Mostly **fine**, but **restless** and tight on money.

fieldNote: Vera uses AI **every day** and sees it as a way to outpace graduates.
Her **entrepreneurial** streak shows even in the calmest picture.
She'd ask her manager first, valuing **loyalty** over a quick win.

steps.text: Push Philip for her own sign-off limit on deals
Sell small packs of compostable boxes at the Saturday market
Rebuild savings a little every month after the wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is a chance, and people who work hard will find their place. I'd tell my friends at church to learn the tools instead of fearing them. I wouldn't ask the government to fix it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my junior job shrinks fast. The AI already does half of what I do at Cresta, the packaging distributor, and the managers would see that. But I'm the one who knows how to use it, and I've got the market traders, so I've got options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make myself the person at Cresta who runs the AI buying, and ask for it in writing. I'd grow the Saturday packaging stall into a small online shop for food trucks. And Daniel and I would put every spare penny back into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but more excited than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to Daniel's job in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Driving's hands-on, so he's fine for now. Maybe the route planning changes, but he still drives the lorry. That's a comfort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if Cresta cut people?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really. Firms have to compete. I'd only be angry if they didn't give people a chance to learn first.

say: I'd say change is **a chance** for people who work hard.
I'd tell church friends to **learn the tools** instead of fearing them.
think: My junior job **shrinks fast**, since AI already does half of it.
I know the tools and have **market traders**, so I have options.
do: Ask Cresta, **in writing**, to let me run AI buying.
Grow the stall into a small **online shop** for food trucks.
Put every spare penny into **savings** with Daniel.
S1.quote: The AI already does half of what I do at Cresta, the packaging distributor, and the managers would see that.
fieldNote: Vera expects her role to **shrink**, but feels she has options.
She **blames no one**; firms compete, she just wants a chance to learn.
Her husband's **driving job** is a comfort in this picture.

steps.text: Ask Cresta in writing to let her run the AI buying
Turn the market stall into an online shop for food trucks
Put spare money into savings each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a shock, and families and churches will need to stick together. I'd say work hard and adapt. I don't think waiting for the government is the answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my Cresta job is gone by 2028, and my edge with the tools goes with it. Daniel's lorry job lasts until about 2031, which gives us three years of his wage. My packaging business would be the only thing I own, and AI helps small sellers too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go full time on the packaging business as soon as Cresta lets me go, or before. I'd use AI for all the admin, ordering and the website, so it's just me and the stock. We'd cut everything, sell my car, and not have children yet, even though we wanted to start soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. But I'd be busy, and busy helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Daniel about children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not having a baby yet is not no, it's not yet. Having a baby with no income would be foolish. Daniel would be sad, he wants to be a dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about 2031, when robots can drive and stack shelves?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then Daniel's job goes too. I'd hope the business is strong by then. I don't know if that's enough.

say: I'd say families and churches must **stick together**.
I'd say work hard and adapt, rather than **wait for government**.
think: My Cresta job and my **tools edge** are gone by 2028.
Daniel's **lorry job** lasts until about 2031, three more years of wages.
do: Go **full time** on the packaging business when Cresta lets me go.
Use AI for **admin**, ordering and the website.
S2.quote: Not having a baby yet is not no, it's not yet. Having a baby with no income would be foolish.
fieldNote: Vera expects to **lose her job** and leans on Daniel's later robot date.
She'd **delay children**, a painful choice for both of them.
Her business is her **only asset**, and she knows it may not be enough.

steps.text: Run the packaging business full time after leaving Cresta
Use AI for the business admin, ordering and website
Put off having children until there's income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, so use it well. Start something, learn something. I'd say that to young people at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is just right for my business. I could stay at Cresta two or three years, save, and grow the stall into a real shop online. Daniel's job lasts until about 2034, so we'd have his wage underneath us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd keep my Cresta job and run the stall at weekends, and use AI to set up the online shop. I'd save every pound from the stall. We'd plan to start a family in a couple of years, once the business makes something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Positive, with a bit of fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you leave Cresta?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When my market stall makes half my salary, I'll leave the packaging distributor, even if it's risky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you worry about most here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big online sellers with better AI undercutting me. That's the real fight.

I'd tell young people at church to **start something** or learn something.
think: Five years is **just right** to grow the stall into a real online shop.
Daniel's wage lasts until about **2034**, underneath us.
do: Keep the Cresta job and run the **stall at weekends**.
Use AI to set up the **online shop** and save every pound from it.
Plan to start a **family** in a couple of years.
S3.quote: When my market stall makes half my salary, I'll leave the packaging distributor, even if it's risky.
fieldNote: Five years fits Vera's plan to **grow her business** before quitting.
She has a **clear trigger**: stall income at half her salary.
Her biggest fear is **bigger sellers** with better AI.

steps.text: Run the packaging stall every weekend

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a blessing, so no excuses. Build something. I'd tell everyone I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means I could get promoted at Cresta, build the business slowly, and have children. By 2036 I'd have a proper little company. Daniel's lorry is safe till about 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd focus on the Cresta job and get my sign-off limit. I'd keep the stall going at weekends. We'd start trying for a baby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful. Still careful with money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your business to look like in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three or four staff, a small warehouse, selling to cafés in three towns. AI doing the paperwork. Me doing the deals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you hire people or use AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. In my business I'd want real people from church and the market, but I'd use AI for the screen work.

I'd tell everyone I know to **build something**.
think: Ten years lets me get **promoted**, build the business and have children.
By **2036** I'd have a proper little company, with Daniel safe till 2039.
do: Focus on Cresta and win my **sign-off limit**.
Start trying for **a baby** with Daniel.
S4.quote: In my business I'd want real people from church and the market, but I'd use AI for the screen work.
fieldNote: With ten years Vera's plans are **expansive**: promotion, business and a baby.
She'd **hire people** from her community and use AI for paperwork.
Thin savings keep her from **calm**, even here.

steps.text: Win a sign-off limit for deals at Cresta
Keep the packaging stall running every weekend
Start trying for a baby with Daniel

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be launching a business with no savings and putting off a family. What would help is small loans for people starting businesses, and simple rules so small sellers aren't crushed by big firms with better AI.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about faith and community. People like me will lean on church and family, not just government, when the work goes. Those places will need strength too.

headlineQuote: People like me will lean on church and family, not just government, when the work goes.
portrait: Vera is a **27-year-old** junior buyer of paper and card packaging, newly married to lorry driver Daniel.
She uses AI **every day** and hopes it will help her outpace buyers with degrees.
After the wedding they have **under a month** of savings.
In every picture she builds a **packaging business**, starting at a Saturday market stall.
She blames no one, trusts **family and church**, and would delay children only in the fastest picture.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd launch a business with no savings and put off a family.
whatWouldHelp: **Small loans** for new businesses, and simple rules protecting small sellers from big firms.
